extracted.intended_audience: political theorists, constitutional designers, statesmen, and educated readers interested in republican government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and argues principles for structuring republican governments to secure liberty and justice — especially the need for fixed laws, separation of powers, bicameralism, and institutional checks to counter natural inequalities and human passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed constitution and stated laws
rubrics_metrics.description: "Neither liberty nor justice can be secured to the individuals of a nation, nor its prosperity promoted, but by a fixed constitution of government and stated laws, known and obeyed by all."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page insists a free society requires laws that are fixed, known, and generally obeyed; without such laws government degenerates into the mere will and pleasure of men. This is presented as a first principle for securing liberty and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government of laws, not of men
rubrics_metrics.description: "Legitimate government consists only in the dominion of equal laws, made with common consent, and not in the dominion of any men over other men."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited classical authorities (Aristotle, Livy, Harrington, Sidney) are invoked to support the maxim that law must prevail over personal commands; laws must be the controlling principle rather than individual rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil liberty as self-government by common consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Price's definition: "the power of a civil society to govern itself, by its own discretion, or by laws of its own making, by the majority, in a collective body, or by fair representation. In every free state, every man is his own legislator."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses the ideal that citizens govern themselves through laws made by common consent or representation. The author notes this is a useful definition but also points out its limits (see criterion about public good and protection of minorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must promote the general interest / public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Add to equal laws by common consent this other — that they be for the general interest or the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that unanimous or majority-made laws can still be harmful if they do not pursue the public good (gives examples such as restrictive religious/holiday laws or navigation acts). Thus constitutions should aim laws at general welfare, not merely majority will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of two assemblies and a third branch (separation of powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: To demonstrate the necessity of two assemblies in the legislature, as well as of a third branch in it, to defend the executive authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues a single assembly concentrating legislative, executive, and judicial authority will become aristocratic, then oligarchic, and finally tyrannical; therefore bicameralism plus a distinct executive (and other checks) are required to secure liberty and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural checks to prevent aristocratic encroachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose: throw aristocratic elements into one assembly; keep executive power entirely out of their hands as a body; erect a first magistrate invested with the whole executive authority; make them dependent on that magistrate for public executive employments; give that magistrate a negative on the legislature; erect on the other side a house of commons fairly, fully, and adequately representing the people, who shall have the power of negativing their attempts and of withholding supplies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a multi-part prescription for institutional design: concentrate aristocratic influence into one legislative chamber while denying them executive control; empower a chief magistrate with veto/negative; and create a popular chamber with real powers (vetoing attempts and withholding funds) to counterbalance the aristocratic chamber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offices open equally; merit and conduct required
rubrics_metrics.description: "While every office is equally open to every competitor... some men must take more pains to deserve and acquire an office than others, and must behave better in it, or they will not hold it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes formal equality of access to office but also that practical merit, effort, and behaviour determine who succeeds and retains office. This balances openness with expectations of conduct and competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for natural aristocracy and inequalities in constitutional design
rubrics_metrics.description: "These sources of inequality, which are common to every people... this natural aristocracy among mankind, has been dilated on, because it is a fact: essential to be considered in the institution of a government."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Birth, fortune, reputation, talents create persistent inequalities; constitutions must acknowledge and channel these realities so that the advantages they confer can benefit society without becoming dangerous to public liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of a single assembly (tendency to aristocracy/oligarchy/tyranny)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single assembly, without counterpoise, balance, or equilibrium, is to have all authority... What is there to restrain them from making tyrannical laws, in order to execute them in a tyrannical manner? ... the single assembly will, upon the first day of its existence, be an aristocracy; in a few days or years... an oligarchy; and then it will soon divide into two or three parties... the victorious general will govern without or with the advice of any council or assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author predicts the progressive corruption of a unitary legislature: concentration of power breeds faction, ambition, and eventual domination. This is offered as an argument for structural separation and checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral jealousy is an unreliable check on representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: "Will it be pretended, that the jealousy and vigilance of the people, and their power to discard them at the next election, will restrain them? ... a jealousy between the electors and the elected neither ought to exist, nor is possible to exist."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that reliance on voter vigilance or future elections is illusory because electors must trust their representatives to select them; therefore structural institutional checks are required rather than sole dependence on electoral punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human passions require institutional restraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions are unlimited; nature has left them so... The love of gold grows faster than the heap of acquisition: the love of praise increases by every gratification... ambition strengthens at every advance... If they surrender the guidance to any one passion, they may depend upon finding it, in the end, an usurping, domineering, cruel tyrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because human appetites (avarice, ambition, love of praise) grow with indulgence and can dominate reason, constitutional design must prevent concentration of power and provide mutual restraints to curb these passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must include counterbalances and channels of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: An assembly composed largely of the rich, honourable, and meritorious will replicate inequalities in society and be naturally divided into parts (a leading genius, a second class resembling him, and a third of followers) — producing envy, faction, and influence-patronage networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of representative bodies should anticipate social stratification and the formation of patronage networks; institutional counterbalances (multiple chambers, checks, limits on executive control) help prevent capture and undue influence.
